title: The Shawshank Redemption
author: Frank Darabont
setting: Shawshank, a fictional state prison in Maine, USA, from 1947 to 1966, with a final journey to the Pacific coast of Mexico in 1967.
gist: Andy Dufresne, a banker wrongly convicted of murdering his wife and her lover, is sent to Shawshank prison, where he becomes friends with Red, a long-serving prisoner who narrates the film. Over nearly twenty years Andy survives brutality and a corrupt, Bible-quoting warden, keeps hope alive, and finally escapes and exposes the warden; Red, released on parole, follows him to Mexico. Frank Darabont wrote and directed the film from Stephen King's novella 'Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption'.

people.name: Andy Dufresne
people.who: A quiet, educated banker sentenced to two life sentences for murdering his wife and her lover, a crime he did not commit.
people.wants: Freedom, and to keep hope alive.

people.name: Ellis 'Red' Redding
people.who: A long-serving prisoner who can smuggle in almost anything; Andy's closest friend and the film's narrator.
people.wants: Parole; later, to see Andy again.
people.end: He breaks parole and joins Andy on the beach.
people.trait: Wry and worn down, then hopeful

people.name: Warden Samuel Norton
people.who: The Bible-quoting warden who secretly grows rich through corruption and uses Andy to hide his money.
people.trait: Holy on the outside, corrupt inside

people.name: Captain Byron Hadley
people.who: The brutal captain of the guards, who rules the prisoners through violence.

people.name: Brooks Hatlen
people.who: The elderly prison librarian, inside for about fifty years, who cannot cope when he is released.
people.wants: To stay inside, where he belongs.
people.end: He hangs himself after his release.
people.trait: Gentle and lost outside the walls

people.name: Tommy Williams
people.who: A young thief who arrives in 1965; Andy helps him study, and Tommy turns out to know who really committed Andy's crime.
people.wants: His exam, and a way out.

people.name: Heywood
people.who: One of Red's group of friends, who taunts the new arrivals on Andy's first night.
people.wants: A laugh at the new arrivals.

people.name: Bogs Diamond
people.who: Leader of 'the Sisters', a gang that repeatedly attacks Andy in his early years in prison.
people.end: Hadley beats him and he's moved away.

moments.title: The crime and the trial
moments.what: At night, a drunk Andy sits in his car outside the house where his wife is with her lover, loading a revolver; these images are cut together with his trial, where he insists he threw the gun into a river. He is convicted of both murders and given two life sentences.
moments.why: The film opens in darkness and injustice, and the cross-cutting between the night and the courtroom leaves the viewer unsure at first whether Andy is guilty.
tell: Night. A man sits in his car, drunk, outside the house where his wife is with her lover. He's loading a revolver.
This is Andy Dufresne, a banker. The film cuts between this night and his trial, where he swears he threw the gun into a river.
The jury doesn't believe him. Two murders. Two life sentences.

chain.happens: Drunk, with a gun, outside his wife's lover's house; Andy is convicted of their murders.
chain.shows: Justice can fail, and an innocent man loses everything.
chain.leads: Andy is sent to Shawshank for life.

moments.title: Red's first parole hearing
moments.what: Twenty years into a life sentence, Red tells the parole board he is a changed man, and his file is stamped 'REJECTED'. In voiceover he introduces himself as the prisoner who can get things smuggled into Shawshank.
moments.why: It sets up the parole hearings that measure Red's journey, and introduces the voiceover through which we see the whole story.
tell: Meet Red. Twenty years into a life sentence, telling the parole board he's a changed man.
Rejected.
Red is our narrator, and the man in Shawshank who can get you things, smuggled in from outside.

chain.happens: After twenty years, Red's parole is rejected.
chain.shows: The system decides who counts as 'rehabilitated', and hope is rationed.
chain.leads: Red, our narrator, is still inside when Andy arrives.

moments.title: Welcome to Shawshank
moments.where: Early in the film: Andy's first night
moments.what: Warden Norton tells the new prisoners that he believes in discipline and the Bible. That night Heywood and other prisoners taunt the new arrivals until one breaks down in tears; Captain Hadley beats him, he dies in the infirmary, and the next morning Andy, who made no sound all night, asks what the dead man's name was.
moments.why: It shows the cruelty and indifference of the institution, and Andy's quiet humanity in the middle of it.
tell: New men arrive. Warden Norton tells them he believes in two things: discipline and the Bible.
That night the old prisoners taunt the new ones until one breaks down in tears. Captain Hadley beats him, and he dies in the infirmary.
Andy makes no sound all night. In the morning he asks one question: what was the dead man's name?

chain.happens: Norton's welcome, and a new prisoner is beaten to death on the first night.
chain.shows: Shawshank runs on cruelty and fear.

moments.title: Beer on the roof
moments.what: While tarring the roof of the licence-plate factory, Andy overhears Captain Hadley complaining about tax on an inheritance and dares to offer advice; Hadley nearly throws him off the roof, but Andy explains how to keep the money legally tax-free, asking only for three beers each for his fellow workers. The men drink in the sunshine while Andy sits apart, smiling, and Red's voiceover says they felt like free men.
moments.why: Andy discovers that his knowledge is a kind of power, and the prisoners briefly experience ordinary freedom.
tell: Andy is tarring a roof when he hears Captain Hadley complaining about tax on an inheritance. So he offers advice.
Hadley nearly throws him off the roof. But Andy explains how to keep the money legally, and asks for one thing in return: three beers each for his workmates.
The men drink in the sun. Andy sits apart, smiling. For a moment, they feel like free men.

chain.happens: Andy's tax advice wins beers for the men tarring the roof.
chain.shows: Andy's brains give him a little power, and the men a little dignity.
chain.leads: Andy becomes useful to the guards.

moments.title: Brooks is released
moments.where: Around the middle of the film
moments.what: When the elderly librarian Brooks Hatlen learns he is to be paroled after fifty years, he holds a knife to Heywood's throat in the hope of being kept inside, and Red explains that Brooks is 'institutionalized'. Outside, Brooks cannot cope with the changed world, and he hangs himself in his halfway-house room after carving 'Brooks was here' into a wooden beam.
moments.why: It shows that prison can destroy a man's ability to live in freedom, a fate Red himself later fears.
tell: Brooks Hatlen, the old librarian, is getting parole after fifty years. And he's terrified.
He holds a knife to Heywood's throat, hoping they'll keep him inside. Red explains: Brooks is 'institutionalized'.
Outside, the world has moved on without him. He can't cope. In his halfway-house room he carves his name into a beam, and hangs himself.

chain.happens: Brooks is paroled after fifty years, and hangs himself outside.
chain.shows: Institutionalisation: prison can make freedom unbearable.
chain.leads: Red fears the same will happen to him.

moments.title: Mozart over the loudspeakers
moments.where: Around the middle of the film
moments.what: Andy's years of letters finally win a small grant and boxes of donated books and records for the library; he locks himself in the office and plays a duet from Mozart's 'The Marriage of Figaro' over the loudspeakers, and the prisoners stand still in the yard to listen. He is given two weeks in solitary, and afterwards tells the men that music is something inside that cannot be taken from them, while Red warns that hope is a dangerous thing.
moments.why: It is the film's clearest image of inner freedom, and it begins the argument about hope that runs to the final scene.
tell: Years of letters, and finally: a small grant, and boxes of donated books and records for the library.
Andy locks himself in the office and plays Mozart over the loudspeakers. The whole yard stops to listen.
It costs him two weeks in solitary. Worth it, he says: music is something inside that they can't take from you. Red isn't so sure. Hope, he warns, is a dangerous thing.

chain.happens: Andy plays Mozart over the loudspeakers to the whole prison.
chain.shows: Beauty and hope can't be locked up.
chain.leads: Solitary for Andy, and Red's warning that hope is dangerous.

moments.title: Tommy's evidence
moments.what: Tommy, a young prisoner Andy is helping to study, reveals that a former cellmate boasted of killing a golf pro and his lover, the crime Andy was convicted of. Warden Norton, who relies on Andy to hide his illegal profits, refuses to help and throws Andy into solitary when he protests, then has Hadley shoot Tommy dead at night and threatens to take away Andy's protection and destroy the library if he stops working for him.
moments.why: The institution destroys justice to protect corrupt power, pushing Andy to the edge.
moments.quote: How can you be so obtuse?
tell: Tommy, a young prisoner Andy is helping to study, tells a story: an old cellmate once boasted of killing a golf pro and his lover.
That's Andy's crime. Someone else did it.
But Andy is too useful to Warden Norton, who needs him to hide his illegal money. Norton throws Andy into solitary, has Hadley shoot Tommy dead, and threatens to destroy everything Andy has built.

chain.happens: Tommy could prove Andy innocent, and Norton has him shot.
chain.leads: Andy loses his last legal hope.

moments.title: 'Get busy living'
moments.where: Final third of the film, after Andy leaves solitary
moments.what: Andy tells Red that he was a distant husband who drove his wife away, though he did not kill her, describes his dream of running a small hotel in Zihuatanejo, Mexico, and makes Red promise that if he is ever freed he will look under a rock by a stone wall in a hayfield near Buxton. When Red hears that Andy has asked for a length of rope, he fears Andy is planning to kill himself.
moments.why: It frames the film's central choice between hope and despair.
moments.quote: Get busy living, or get busy dying.
tell: Out of solitary, Andy sits with Red against the wall. He admits he was a distant husband who drove his wife away. But he didn't kill her.
He talks about a dream: a little hotel in Zihuatanejo, Mexico. And he makes Red promise to look under a rock by a stone wall in a hayfield near Buxton.
Then Red hears that Andy has asked for a length of rope, and fears the worst.

chain.happens: Andy tells Red to 'get busy living', and about the rock near Buxton.

moments.title: The empty cell
moments.what: At the morning count Andy's cell is empty; in a rage the warden throws a stone at the poster on the wall, and it tears straight through, revealing a tunnel. Red's voiceover and a flashback show that Andy dug through the wall in less than twenty years with his small rock hammer and, during a thunderstorm, crawled through five hundred yards of sewer pipe to freedom, raising his arms in the rain.
moments.why: The film's great reversal turns Andy's years of patience into an act of hidden defiance, and gives the film its central image of freedom.
tell: Morning count. Andy's cell is empty.
The warden throws a stone at the poster on the wall, and it goes straight through. Behind it: a tunnel.
Red tells us how. Less than twenty years with a little rock hammer. Then, in a thunderstorm, five hundred yards of sewer pipe. And Andy, arms raised in the rain, free.

chain.happens: Andy's cell is empty, and the poster hides a tunnel.
chain.shows: Patience and hope beat the system.

moments.title: The warden's fall
moments.what: Posing as 'Randall Stephens', the false identity he had invented to hide Norton's money, Andy withdraws it from several banks and posts the warden's account book and evidence of his crimes to a newspaper. As police arrive, Hadley is arrested, and Norton opens his safe, hidden behind the embroidered words 'His judgment cometh and that right early', to find Andy's Bible with the rock hammer's hiding place cut into its pages, before shooting himself.
moments.why: Corrupt power collapses, and justice arrives through Andy's cleverness and the press rather than through the courts.
tell: Remember the person Andy invented to hide Norton's money? Andy becomes him, and empties the accounts.
He posts the warden's account book and the proof of his crimes to a newspaper. The police arrive, and Hadley is arrested.
Norton opens his safe and finds Andy's Bible, with the rock hammer's hiding place cut into its pages. Then he shoots himself.

chain.happens: Andy exposes Norton's crimes, and Norton shoots himself.
chain.shows: Justice catches up with the corrupt at last.
chain.leads: Hadley is arrested, and Norton's power is gone.

moments.title: Red's last hearing
moments.where: Near the end of the film (1967)
moments.what: After forty years, Red tells the parole board that 'rehabilitated' is just a made-up word, that he regrets the foolish young man who committed his crime, and that he no longer cares what they decide; this time he is released. Outside, he is given Brooks's old room and a job bagging groceries, as Brooks had, asks his manager's permission to go to the toilet, and admits he thinks about breaking parole to be sent back.
moments.why: Red's honesty finally frees him, but life outside shows how deeply the institution has shaped him.
tell: Forty years in, Red faces the board again. And this time he stops performing.
'Rehabilitated' is just a made-up word, he says. He regrets the foolish young man he was, and he doesn't care what they decide. Released.
Outside, he gets Brooks's old room and a job bagging groceries, as Brooks had. He asks permission to go to the toilet. And he thinks about breaking parole, just to be sent back.

chain.happens: Red is released, and struggles outside just as Brooks did.
chain.leads: Red chooses Andy's path instead of Brooks's.

moments.title: Buxton and Zihuatanejo
moments.what: Keeping his promise, Red finds the box Andy hid under the rock near Buxton, with money and a letter inviting him to Mexico; he carves 'So was Red' beside Brooks's words, breaks parole and takes a bus south. In the final scene he walks along a sunlit beach at Zihuatanejo to Andy, who is working on an old boat, and the camera pulls back over the blue Pacific.
moments.why: The ending rewards hope and friendship, and shows Red choosing life instead of becoming another Brooks.
moments.quote: Hope is a good thing, maybe the best of things, and no good thing ever dies.
tell: Red keeps his promise. Under the rock near Buxton he finds a box: money, and a letter inviting him to Mexico.
He carves 'So was Red' beside Brooks's words, breaks parole, and takes a bus south.
The last scene: a sunlit beach, Andy working on an old boat, and Red walking towards him. The camera pulls back over the blue Pacific.

chain.happens: Red finds Andy's letter and joins him in Zihuatanejo.
chain.leads: The film ends in freedom, by the open sea.

themes.name: Power and control
points: Official power at Shawshank is brutal: Warden Norton greets new prisoners with talk of discipline and the Bible, and that night Captain Hadley beats a frightened prisoner to death, with no one held to account [shawshank-3].
Andy finds a quieter power in knowledge: by offering tax advice, he turns Hadley, who nearly threw him off the roof, into the man who supplies his fellow prisoners with beer [shawshank-4].
The warden will kill to keep control: when Tommy's evidence could free Andy, the man who hides his illegal profits, Norton has Hadley shoot Tommy dead [shawshank-7].
Andy finally turns the warden's own system against him, using the false identity he created to hide Norton's money to take that money himself, and Norton's power collapses [shawshank-10].

themes.name: Freedom and entrapment
points: Prison traps the mind as well as the body: Brooks, 'institutionalized' after fifty years, cannot live in the free world and hangs himself [shawshank-5].

Freedom can be felt even inside the walls: when Andy plays Mozart over the loudspeakers, the prisoners stand still to listen, and Red's voiceover says that for a brief moment every man in Shawshank felt free [shawshank-6].
Andy's escape through five hundred yards of sewer pipe ends in the film's great image of freedom, as he stands with his arms raised in the pouring rain [shawshank-9].
Release is not the same as freedom: on parole, Red still asks permission to go to the toilet [shawshank-11], and he becomes truly free only when he breaks parole to follow Andy [shawshank-12].

themes.name: Courage and silence
points: Andy shows quiet courage from his first night: he makes no sound while another man breaks down, and the next morning he asks the dead prisoner's name while the others shrug off the killing [shawshank-3].
Andy risks his life to speak up to Hadley on the roof [shawshank-4], and accepts solitary confinement rather than switch off the Mozart [shawshank-6].
Speaking the truth is punished: Andy is thrown into solitary for challenging the warden, and Tommy is shot after agreeing to testify [shawshank-7].
Red's courage is to stop pretending: at his final hearing he refuses to say what the board wants to hear [shawshank-11], and he breaks parole rather than give in to despair [shawshank-12].

aspects.name: Power and authority
points: The warden's authority is total and claims the backing of religion: Norton tells new arrivals that he believes in discipline and the Bible [shawshank-3].
The guards' violence goes unchecked: Hadley beats a prisoner to death on Andy's first night [shawshank-3] and later shoots Tommy on the warden's orders [shawshank-7].
Authority can be bargained with by a prisoner who has something it wants: Andy's financial skill wins beer for his fellow workers [shawshank-4].
This corrupt authority is brought down from outside: once Andy's evidence reaches a newspaper, Hadley is arrested and Norton shoots himself [shawshank-10].

aspects.name: Class, money and status
points: Andy's education as a banker gives him value even in prison, where his tax advice to Hadley wins privileges for his friends [shawshank-4].
Prison has its own economy and status: Red is respected as the man who can get things [shawshank-2].
Money corrupts the institution: Norton relies on Andy to hide his illegal profits, so he will not let Tommy's evidence set Andy free [shawshank-7].
Status depends on the institution: inside, Brooks is the respected librarian, but outside he is an old man bagging groceries in a world that has no use for him [shawshank-5].

aspects.name: Gender roles and marriage
points: Shawshank is an almost entirely male world where toughness is expected: a new prisoner who weeps on his first night is mocked and then beaten to death [shawshank-3].
Marriage appears only as failure: the film opens with the story of Andy's wife's affair and murder [shawshank-1], and Andy later admits he was a distant husband who drove her away [shawshank-8].
Women are present mostly as images and voices: the film-star posters on Andy's wall, the last of which hides his tunnel [shawshank-9], and the two women's voices singing Mozart [shawshank-6].

aspects.name: Religion and the Church
points: Religion is used as a tool of control: Norton presents himself as a man of the Bible when he welcomes new prisoners [shawshank-3].
The film exposes this as hypocrisy: the Bible-quoting warden runs a corrupt business and arranges a murder [shawshank-7].

Andy turns the warden's faith against him: Norton's safe, hidden behind the embroidered words 'His judgment cometh and that right early', holds Andy's Bible, with the rock hammer's hiding place cut into its pages [shawshank-10].
The 'redemption' of the title comes through hope and friendship rather than through the Church [shawshank-12].

aspects.name: Family and community
points: Prisoners build their own community: Red's group of friends becomes Andy's substitute family, and on the roof he wins them a moment of ordinary life [shawshank-4].
Losing that community can be fatal: Brooks, cut off from the only world he knows, dies alone outside [shawshank-5].
Andy builds community through education, building up the prison library and helping young Tommy to study [shawshank-7].
The film ends with a chosen family, as Red travels to Mexico to be reunited with his friend [shawshank-12].

aspects.name: Law, institutions and justice
points: The legal system fails from the start: Andy is convicted of two murders he did not commit and given two life sentences [shawshank-1].
Parole is shown as an empty ritual: Red is rejected when he says what the board wants to hear [shawshank-2] and released only when he speaks honestly and says he does not care [shawshank-11].
The institution blocks justice: when Tommy offers new evidence, the warden destroys it by having the witness killed [shawshank-7].
Justice comes from outside the system, through Andy's escape and the evidence he sends to a newspaper [shawshank-10].

aspects.name: Race and the outsider
points: The film says almost nothing directly about race: Red is a Black man and Andy a white former banker, yet their friendship becomes the heart of the film without the film ever making race an issue [shawshank-12].
Andy is an outsider by class and temperament: educated and reserved, he sits apart on the roof, not drinking, while the others enjoy the beer he won for them [shawshank-4].

Long imprisonment turns men into outsiders in the free world: Brooks finds that the world has changed too fast for him [shawshank-5], and Red, given Brooks's old room, fears the same fate [shawshank-11].

gvv.opening: The film opens in darkness and injustice: an innocent man is sentenced to life, Red is refused parole, and on Andy's first night a frightened prisoner is beaten to death, suggesting a world without hope.
gvv.ending: It ends in bright sunlight on a Mexican beach as Red and Andy are reunited; the corrupt warden has fallen and hope and friendship have won, though only by escaping a system that never delivered justice.
points: Darabont contrasts dark and light visually: the grey, enclosed prison and night scenes such as Tommy's killing [shawshank-7] give way to the open, sunlit blue of the Pacific in the final shot [shawshank-12].
The film admits that hope can be crushed: Brooks hangs himself after his release [shawshank-5], and Tommy is killed for being willing to tell the truth [shawshank-7].
Moments of grace inside the walls, such as the beer on the roof [shawshank-4] and the Mozart broadcast [shawshank-6], suggest that the human spirit cannot be fully imprisoned.

Red's voiceover guides our feelings: we share his slow journey from warning that hope is dangerous [shawshank-6], to repeating Andy's choice to 'get busy living' [shawshank-8], to ending the film with the words 'I hope' [shawshank-12].

The ending suggests that institutions are corrupt but individuals can be good: justice comes not from the courts or the parole board but from Andy's patience and the truth he sends to a newspaper [shawshank-10].
The escape is hidden from the viewer as well as from Red, so its sudden reveal gives us the same shock and delight [shawshank-9].
